blocks.heading: Primary, secondary and tertiary activity
blocks.text: Activity sectors classify what is done. Primary businesses obtain natural resources; secondary businesses transform materials into products or carry out construction; tertiary businesses supply services. Follow the activity rather than the owner or product’s final user. Growing mahangu is primary, milling it into flour is secondary, and transporting or selling the flour is tertiary. Transport does not physically manufacture the flour even though it adds value by making it available where needed. A business can operate in more than one activity sector. An enterprise growing fruit, making juice and running its own shop has primary, secondary and tertiary operations. If asked to classify one operation, classify that operation. If describing the whole enterprise, explain its combination rather than assuming a single label covers every stage. Public/private ownership is a separate axis: a privately owned farm is both private sector and primary sector. Development of services does not remove the economy’s need for materials or manufactured goods; the sectors supply inputs and customers to one another.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Osha Clay extracts clay near Otjiwarongo, Imba Pots shapes and fires it, and Hela Couriers delivers the pots to buyers. Extraction is primary; changing clay into pots is secondary; delivery is tertiary. A privately owned courier remains tertiary even if a public school buys its service. Classifying the process avoids confusing a customer’s ownership with a supplier’s activity.

blocks.heading: Primary sector
blocks.text: The primary sector obtains natural resources from the land or sea. Farming, fishing, forestry and mineral extraction are examples. The classification concerns extraction or harvesting, before manufacturing transforms the resource into another product. Selling what a farm grows does not make the growing activity tertiary.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Luma Farm grows vegetables near Rundu. A separate factory cans them. Growing the vegetables is primary. The later canning is secondary because the factory processes the resource. Distinguish stages instead of giving all food-related activity one label.

blocks.heading: Secondary sector
blocks.text: The secondary sector transforms materials into manufactured products and includes construction. It takes inputs such as timber, flour or metal and changes them into an output such as a desk, loaf or gate. Being secondary does not mean less important; the term identifies the stage of activity. Delivery of a finished product is a separate service activity.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ondira Frames purchases timber and makes window frames. The transformation from timber to frames is secondary. If another business merely sells the frames unchanged, its retail activity is tertiary.

blocks.heading: Tertiary sector
blocks.text: The tertiary sector provides services to consumers or other businesses. Retailing, transport, banking and repair services are examples. A service may support physical goods without manufacturing them: a carrier moves an existing product and a shop makes it available to buyers. A business’s classification follows its service activity rather than whether its customer is public or private.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Kina Deliveries transports parcels between shops and households. Moving the parcels is a tertiary activity. Kina is not a primary producer simply because one parcel contains farm produce.
